sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic image editors decompose complex requests into steps, but when a step fails, they mostly retry with the same narrow set of tools and a judge that scores each output by eye directly. We argue that such agents are bounded by two spaces: the action space of what the agent can do, and the observation space of what its judge can see. On our expert-annotated benchmark, a general-purpose editor yields no usable result in over 40% of the cases, and no judge is reliable across edit types. We present EditAgent, which expands both spaces. It routes each step to general editors and specialized methods, and attaches to each candidate a verification record. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models. Candidates are generated in parallel and judged in one listwise call: experts prefer this to sequential refinement in 78.5% of decided comparisons, at no more than half the judge calls. EditAgent improves two open-weight editors on three benchmarks and serves as a data engine for training stronger editors.

sections.content: EditAgent: Rethinking Agentic Image Editing Haiyang Xu1 Yuanjun Xiong2 Tianyu Wang2 Jianming Zhang2 Jialu Li2 Jiteng Mu2 Zhuowen Tu Mingze Xu2 2Adobe Research 1UC San Diego hax038@ucsd.edu; mingzex@adobe.com Figure 1. EditAgent expands both the action space of the agent and the observation space of its judge. Instead of trying again with the same editor, EditAgent generates candidates with different editing methods in parallel, and judge (off-the-shelf VLM) compares them in one call with verification record (evidence) for each candidate, without judge finetuning.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 1. Introduction Agentic image editors decompose complex requests into steps, but when step fails, they mostly retry with the same narrow set of tools and judge that scores each output by eye directly. We argue that such agents are bounded by two spaces: the action space of what the agent can do, and the observation space of what its judge can see. On our expertannotated benchmark, general-purpose editor yields no usable result in over 40% of the cases, and no judge is reliable across edit types. We present EditAgent, which expands both spaces. It routes each step to general editors and specialized methods, and attaches to each candidate verification record. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models. Candidates are generated in parallel and judged in one listwise call: experts prefer this to sequential refinement in 78.5% of decided comparisons, at no more than half the judge calls. EditAgent improves two open-weight editors on three benchmarks and serves as data engine for training stronger editors. *Work done during an internship at Adobe Research. Instruction-based image editing models can now perform wide range of edits from single text instruction [4, 25, 63]. Real requests, however, rarely ask for single edit. Given move me to the left of the frame, widen the shot to show more of the beach, remove the people walking behind me, and make it look like sunset, todays editors tend to complete some parts and silently drop others [57, 67]. Agentic editing systems [15, 30, 49, 75] address this by decomposing the request into steps and running plan-edit-judge loop on each. Yet when step fails, they mostly try again. The step is refined, retried, or rolled back with the same tools and judge. Here we ask the question: when an editing agent fails, is another attempt really what it needs? If not, what does the agent really needs? Consider how professional retoucher would handle the same request: pick different tool for each part, and check each result by zooming in and comparing before and after. retoucher does not simply try again but acts differently and looks more closely. We argue that an editing agent is likewise bounded by two spaces: its action space, what it can do, and its judges observation space, what it can see. Existing agents [15, 30, 49] keep both small. Each attempt runs one tool, often general editor [14, 25, 27, 43, 63], and the judge scores that single output by eye, given only the source image, the edited image and the instruction. To explore how each space should be designed, we introduce diagnostic benchmark of 600 candidate sets over 30 edit types, labeled blindly by professional Photoshop editors  (Fig. 2)  . We find that the general editor yields no usable result in 42.7% of the sets, mostly in geometry, tone and enhancement edits, and specialized method recovers 175 of these 256 failures. Meanwhile, no judge we test, including finetuned reward models [35, 65], is the most accurate across edit groups. We therefore rethink agentic editing by expanding both spaces. Our system, EditAgent, shown in Fig. 1, expands the action space by routing each step to general-purpose editors and specialized methods, including masked local editing, object removal and movement, photometric and geometric operators, and so on. It expands the observation space by attaching to each candidate verification record (evidence), such as change map, close-ups of the edited region, and measured color and geometry, together with the outcomes of programmatic checks, so that the judge knows what code has verified and what remains for visual judgment. Instead of refining one result round after round, EditAgent thus generates candidates from all selected methods in parallel from the same source image, and the judge compares them with their records in single listwise call. Unlike in text-to-image generation [17], professional editors prefer this parallel search over sequential refinement in 78.5% of non-tied comparisons, with at most half the judge calls (Sec. 3.3). With verification records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models without finetuning. Instantiated with Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [63] and FLUX.2-klein-9B [26], EditAgent improves both backbones on EdiVal [6], Complex-Edit [67], and ComplexBenchEdit [57]. Because it accepts only verified edits, EditAgent also serves as data engine. Editors finetuned on its 25.7K accepted sessions outperform those trained on data generated directly by the base editor FLUX.2-klein-9B. Our contributions are threefold. We identify the agents action space and its judges observation space as two bottlenecks of agentic image editing, and analyze both with an expert-annotated diagnostic benchmark spanning 30 edit types. We propose EditAgent, which expands the action space with specialized editing methods and the observation space with verification records, and couples them through parallel candidate generation and listwise judging. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned editing reward models. EditAgent consistently improves strong open-weight editors on three multi-turn and complex-instruction benchmarks, and the sessions it accepts yield training data that further improves standalone editors. 2. Related Work Single-turn Image Editing. Following pioneering diffusionbased methods [16, 19, 37, 39], InstructPix2Pix [4] and Emu Edit [50] established general instruction-based editing. Recent proprietary [14, 43, 48, 60] and open-weight [11, 26, 27, 33, 63, 64] models now provide strong general-purpose editing. Other methods offer more explicit control through masked editing [2, 54], localized text-driven editing [9, 29], or point-based manipulation [51]. EditAgent builds on some of these editors and coordinates them together. Multi-turn Editing and Agentic Editing. MagicBrush [76] provides singleand multi-turn editing trajectories, making the preservation of earlier edits an explicit target. Agentic systems further incorporate planning and feedback, for example by scheduling restoration tools [81], searching and revising cost-aware tool paths [15], and guiding iterative edits with instruction decomposition, visual feedback, or dialogue history [7, 28, 30, 36, 49, 62, 68, 75]. Others integrate reflection into the editing model [73], maintain structured history for long-horizon editing [71], or explore editing trajectories with Monte Carlo tree search [70]. These agents retry within fixed tool set and judge one output at time by eye, whereas EditAgent expands the action space with specialized editing methods and the observation space of its judge with evidence and side-by-side comparison. Evaluation and Benchmarking. Traditional protocols measure edit alignment with CLIP-based text-image or directional similarity [12, 44] and preservation with CLIP or DINO image similarity [5]. Benchmarks further compare outputs with ground-truth target images [76] or assess unedited regions [18] with PSNR, SSIM [61], and LPIPS [77]. More recent protocols prompt VLMs such as GPT-4o [40] and Qwen2.5-VL [3] to rate instruction following, preservation, and perceptual quality [20, 33, 67, 72]. Others augment VLM judgments with visual tools [6, 58] or aggregate automatic scores into human-aligned evaluation [47]. Rather than training dedicated editing reward models [35, 65, 78], we adapt off-the-shelf VLMs with taskspecific verification records. 3. Rethinking Agentic Editing We evaluate both action and observation spaces on the diagnostic benchmark (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2). Specifically, we address three core questions: (1) Does general editor need larger action space or only more samples (Sec. 3.2)? (2) Under fixed budget, should candidates be refined sequentially or generated in parallel (Sec. 3.3)? (3) Can judge that scores one output at time select satisfactory edit (Sec. 3.4)? Figure 2. Where the action space and the observation space fall short, by edit group. (a) Action space: share of the expert-labeled sets in which only general-editor candidates, only specialized candidates, both kinds, or no candidate are usable. (b) Observation space: Winner-Set Hit@1 on the expert-labeled sets with at least one usable candidate. Random is the expected Hit@1 of uniform random pick. 3.1. Diagnostic Benchmark We construct benchmark of 600 editing sets covering 30 fine-grained edit types, with 20 sets per type. The types span six groups: Content, Style & Effects, Scene, Photometric, Geometry, and Enhancement. Each set contains source image, an instruction, and 2-4 candidate edits from two sources: samples of general-purpose editor (FLUX.2-klein9B) and specialized methods such as masked local editing, object removal, and photometric operators. Five professional Photoshop retouchers sit together and select every usable candidate, i.e., every candidate that completes the instruction acceptably. We call the selected candidates the winner set. 3.2. Is One Editor Enough? We categorize the 600 sets by their winner sets (Fig. 2a). The winner set contains only general-editor candidates in 254 sets (42.3%), only specialized candidates in 175 (29.2%), and both kinds in 90 (15.0%). In the remaining 81 sets (13.5%), no candidate is usable. Since every set includes general-editor candidate, the general editor fails in 256 sets (42.7%), and specialized method recovers 175 of them. The outcomes also vary strongly across edit groups. The winner set contains only general-editor candidates in 73.8% of Style & Effects sets, but only specialized candidates in 72.5% of Enhancement and 66.7% of Geometry sets. More samples from the general editor do not recover these failures. For every request, the general editor produces several samples and one of them is delivered, i.e., parallel sampling with verifier [17]. second pool also includes the specialized methods, and the same VLM judge selects the delivered edit in both pools. Both delivered edits are among the labeled candidates of the set. Although the general-editor pool contains more samples, its delivered edit is usable in only 45.2% of the sets, compared with 68.2% for the pool with specialized methods. In the 296 sets where exactly one delivered edit is usable, it comes from the pool with specialized methods in 217. These results show that one editor is not enough, even when sampled more often. 3.3. Refine Sequentially or Search in Parallel? While sequential refinement has been shown to improve textimage alignment in image generation [17], we observe that it can suffer from error accumulation in image editing, as errors introduced in earlier iterations may propagate to later edits. To investigate this, we compare two strategies using the same editor (FLUX.2-klein-9B) and judge (Qwen3.8-27B), each with budget of 4 image generations. Sequential refinement iteratively edits the previous result using prompts revised based on VLM feedback, requiring 3 feedback calls and 1 final selection call. Parallel search, in contrast, generates two candidates independently from the original image. If neither is accepted by the judge, it revises the prompt and generates two more candidates from the original image before selecting the best result. This requires at most 2 VLM calls. In blind comparison on 144 Complex-Edit samples [67] at complexity levels 1, 4, and 8, five professional Photoshop editors preferred parallel search in 102 cases and sequential refinement in 28, with 14 ties. Parallel search thus wins 78.5% of the non-tied comparisons with at most half the VLM calls. Unlike generation, editing must stay faithful to the source image. Sequential refinement keeps editing its own output, so small errors can accumulate, whereas parallel search edits every candidate directly from the source. Thus, for editing, parallel search uses the budget better than sequential refinement. With several candidates available, the delivered edit then depends on what the judge can see. 3.4. Is Judging One Output at Time Enough? We therefore test four judges, each scores one output at time from the source image, the edited image and, except for CLIP-I, the instruction. They are the editing reward models EditScore-72B [35] and EditReward-7B [65], the CLIP-I metric [44] (CLIP similarity to the source image), and Qwen3.8-27B [56] with pass/fail prompt. Winner-Set Hit@1 is the fraction of sets whose top-scoring candidate is in the winner set, i.e., is usable, with ties sharing credit. We report it on the 515 sets with at least one usable candidate. 3 Figure 3. Overview of EditAgent. Bottom: request runs as dependent steps, and each accepted result becomes the source of the next step. Top: step 1, enlarged. (A) The planner orders the steps; the analyzer and router select the applicable methods for the current step. (B) The selected methods generate candidates in parallel from the same source image, each with verification record (evidence). (C) An off-the-shelf VLM compares the candidates with their records and accepts one, or returns feedback for another attempt. Table 1. Comparative judging is better. Overall accuracy (%) on EditReward-Bench [35]. Pointwise scores each candidate alone; listwise (ours) compares them together in one call. Judge Pointwise Listwise (Ours) EditScore-7B EditScore-32B EditScore-72B EditScore-7B, Ensemble@4 EditScore-32B, Ensemble@4 EditScore-72B, Ensemble@4 Qwen3.5-27B Qwen3.8-27B Gemma-4-31B 65.9 68.0 70.3 72.7 73.3 76. 71.7 72.1 73.8 85.2 85.9 86.1 +13.5 +13.8 +12.3 No judge is the most accurate on every group (Fig. 2b). EditScore-72B has the best overall Winner-set Hit@1 but is the best only on Scene, and Qwen3.8-27B, the most accurate on three groups, is only 5.2 points above random on Photometric. CLIP-I, which prefers the candidate closest to the source, shows why. It is the most accurate judge on Photometric and Enhancement, where the correct result changes little, but it is at or below random on Style & Effects and Geometry, where the request requires visible change. What judge must observe therefore depends on the edit. Is preference finetuning the remedy? The EditScore [35] models are trained on large sets of detailed human preference annotations. However, off-the-shelf VLMs can surpass EditScore on its own EditReward-Bench [35] (Tab. 1). EditScore models reach 65.9-70.3%, and with four-pass ensembling [35], EditScore-72B reaches 76.3%. Even judging each candidate alone (pointwise), off-the-shelf VLMs can reach 71.7-73.8%. Furthermore, if we expand the observation space, present candidates side by side in single judge call (listwise), the accuracy can be boosted to 85.2-86.1%. Such comparative judging is not supported by EditScore models, which are finetuned with specific input and output templates. Thus, what judge sees can matter more than how it is trained. Here, comparative judging enables expanded observation space, leading to better judgments. 4. EditAgent Given user request, planner decomposes it into ordered editing steps  (Fig. 3)  . For each step, an analyzer specifies the editing operation and its target, grounder localizes the target with VLM and SAM 2.1 [46] when method needs mask, and router selects the applicable editing methods, each of which generates at least one candidate in parallel (Sec. 4.1). An off-the-shelf VLM judge evaluates the candidates together with their verification records (Sec. 4.2), either accepting one candidate or returning feedback for retry. Each accepted image becomes the source of the next step, and the requirements it satisfies are carried forward so that subsequent turns can verify that they still hold (Sec. 4.3). 4 Table 2. Per-edit-group Winner-Set Hit@1 (%) of Qwen3.8-27B on our diagnostic benchmark. Listwise Evidence Style Content Scene Photo. Geom. Enh. All 84.4 87.1 87.6 81.7 87.1 86.4 67.5 72.0 81.9 54.2 47.2 64. 66.4 78.6 81.4 65.0 71.6 36.8 73.6 80.3 81.3 Figure 4. Examples of the verification record (evidence). (a) close-up of the edited region reveals the blurred checks left by the removal specialist. (b) Measured brightness, clipping and color shift accurately reveal the performance of the photometric operator. 4.1. Expanding the Action Space Candidate Construction. Given an executable instruction and its source image, the analyzer specifies the editing operation and recommends candidate methods, and the router turns the recommendation into set of methods that each contribute at least one candidate. Different methods explore different realizations of the request, while repeated sampling explores variation within method. Action Space. Besides the general editor, the capability pool contains: 1) masked local editing and recoloring, which run the general editor inside SAM 2.1 mask, 2) object removal with OSOR [80], 3) object movement with dedicated model, 4) subject scaling by segmentation and compositing, 5) global and local photometric operators, 6) style filters and neural style transfer, 7) flips, rotations, and rotation to level, and 8) zoom-in by cropping with super-resolution and zoom-out by outpainting. Details can be found in Tab. S5. 4.2. Expanding the Observation Space Comparative Judging. Inspired by Sec. 3.4, we provide the judge with all candidates in one call. It only needs one VLM call per step, whose comparison yields feedback for the next attempt if retry is needed. Verification Records. Just as professional retoucher uses different tools to judge an editing operation, we argue that different edits require checks of different properties  (Fig. 4)  . For example, localized edit requires checking both the target change and the preservation of unrelated content, whereas geometric transformation requires assessing its direction and extent. Some of these properties can be checked 5 Figure 5. Verification record (evidence) further lifts off-the-shelf VLM judge. Winner-Set Hit@1 on our diagnostic benchmark. by code during execution, some require visual judgment. For each candidate, we collect these checks into verification record, together with what remains for visual judgment. EditAgent collects the verification record and gives to the judge, so the judge no longer judges by eye alone. Therefore, after all, the judge will receive the edit instruction, the source image, all candidates and their records in one call. Performance on the Diagnostic Benchmark. To evaluate the effectiveness of the enriched observation space, we report Winner-Set Hit@1 on the 515 candidate sets with at least one usable edit from our diagnostic benchmark (Sec. 3.1), averaged over three runs. Tab. 2 expands the observation space of the Qwen3.8-27B judge in Fig. 2b one step at time. Listwise comparison raises its accuracy from 71.6% to 73.6% and helps on four of the six groups. Comparison alone, however, lowers accuracy on Photometric (from 54.2% to 47.2%) and Enhancement (from 65.0% to 36.8%), the two groups where the correct result changes little from the source (Sec. 3.4). Adding verification records recovers both groups to 64.4% and 80.3%, above the pointwise judge, and raises the overall accuracy to 81.3%, 6.5 points above EditScore72B, the strongest judge in Fig. 2b. Both expansions of the observation space improve the judge, and evidence helps compensate where comparison fails. This gain is not specific to Qwen3.8-27B. As shown in Fig. 5, seven off-the-shelf VLM judges are improved, by 6.3 to 9.3 points. Without records, none of them reaches the finetuned EditScore-72B (74.8%). With records, every one of them exceeds all four finetuned reward models, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 82.8%, 8.0 points above EditScore-72B, the strongest judge in Fig. 2b. Table 3. Complex-Edit [67] comprises 8,496 real and synthetic examples spanning different levels of instruction complexity. ComplexBench-Edit [57] comprises 763 examples with compositional instructions, including parallel constraints and multi-step chains. Together, they assess performance across editing turns, complexity, and compositional structure. Backbones and Baselines. We instantiate EditAgent with two general-purpose editors, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [63] and FLUX.2-klein-9B [26]. For each backbone, we compare standalone editing with its integration into EditAgent. We also compare it with seven agentic editors (Tab. 5). On EdiVal, both backbones edit at the 512 px input resolution. Because most closed-source editors generate at 1024 px or more, we also run Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 at 1024 px and resize back to 512 px for fair comparison. The comparison with agentic editors and all ablations use the 512 px setting. Evaluation. We follow the evaluation rubrics of each benchmark. EdiVal uses its released judges, and Qwen3.827B [56] replaces GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking on Complex-Edit and ComplexBench-Edit. As it is also our internal judge, to avoid potential bias, we additionally evaluate EditAgent using Gemma-4-31B [55] (Tab. S8). Implementation Details. Qwen3.8-27B serves as the planner, analyzer, grounder and judge, and SAM 2.1 [46] turns predicted boxes into masks. Each attempt generates up to three candidates, at least one per applicable method, shown to the judge in random order. Each step allows two retries and each turn two plan revisions. Figure 6. The history check extends what the judge observes to earlier turns. Letting in more daylight in turn 2 clears the frosted glass from turn 1. The history check detects this and repairs. 4.3. Planning and Preserving Edits across Turns The planner splits request into dependent steps when its parts need separate execution, and each accepted step becomes the source of the next. Because the step judge sees one step at time, later edit can undo an earlier one unnoticed. After every turn, history check therefore shows the VLM the original image, the results of earlier turns and the current image, and asks whether each earlier request still holds. On confident violation, EditAgent runs one repair turn and adopts it only if its step judge accepts it  (Fig. 6)  . 5. Experiments 5.1. Experimental Setup Benchmarks. EditAgent as Data Engine Because EditAgent flags every edit that its judge did not accept, its fully accepted sessions can serve as training data. Using FLUX.2-klein-9B as the general editor, EditAgent produces about 25.7K sessions, averaging four turns each. Each session yields one training sample consisting of the source image, session-level instruction, and the final edited image. For comparison, we use FLUX.2-klein-9B to directly edit the same sessions, keeping the training inputs identical and varying only the final images. We fully finetune QwenImage-Edit-2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base-9B on each dataset for one epoch and evaluate them as standalone editors. As shown in Tab. 6, training on EditAgent data improves both editors across all three benchmarks. On EdiVal-O at turn 3, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and FLUX.2-klein-base9B gain 1.95 and 2.00 points, respectively, while their ComplexBench-Edit averages increase by 3.17 and 2.14 points. More importantly, EditAgent data consistently outperforms directly generated FLUX.2-klein-9B data under the same training recipe. Notably, direct FLUX.2-klein-9B data degrades FLUX.2-klein-base-9B on all three benchmarks, whereas EditAgent data improves it. These results suggest that EditAgent provides higher-quality training supervision rather than merely additional training examples. 5.4. Ablation Study Tab. 7 evaluates each component of EditAgent. The vanilla agent, equipped with planning, analysis, history checking, and repair/retry, improves EdiVal-O at turn 3 from 47.64 to 49.43. Expanding the action space yields 2.94-point gain. Sampling the general editor more often does not reproduce this gain. If we replace the action space with copies of the general editor and keep parallel comparison, EdiVal-O reaches 47.53, 48.90, and 49.01 for = 2, 4, and 8. This agrees with the diagnostic study in Sec. 3.2, where restricting EditAgent to the general editor lowers the share of usable delivered edits. Expanding the observation space further improves performance by 3.09 points. 5.5. Qualitative Results Figure 7 compares standalone FLUX.2-klein-9B with EditAgent. Instead, EditAgent judges each step against its source image, which already contains the earlier edits, and checks that they remain. More qualitative comparisons is provided in Sec. I, further demonstrating the overall advantages of our method, even over GPT-Image-2. 6. Conclusion We presented EditAgent, which rethinks agentic image editing as expanding two spaces: the action space of the agent and the observation space of its judge. It routes each step to general-purpose and specialized editing methods, generates their candidates in parallel, and lets the off-the-shelf VLM judge compare them with verification records. EditAgent improves two editing backbones across three benchmarks, and functions as robust data engine, leveraging its accepted sessions to improve standalone editors through fine-tuning. Limitations. EditAgent incurs roughly 10 the inference time of standalone editing models, and its performance is inherently bounded by the capabilities of its underlying editing methods. Nevertheless, EditAgent can serve as data engine for finetuning stronger and more efficient standalone editors, potentially amortizing its computational cost.

The benchmark covers 30 edit types in six groups, with 20 requests per type (Tab. S1). Source images are drawn from COCO val2017 [31], and each image is used in one set only. VLM (Qwen3.8-27B) screens each photograph so that every edit type is assigned only to photographs that support it, and then writes one natural instruction of the assigned type, following the types definition in Tab. Candidates come from two runs of EditAgent on each request, one with the full capability pool and one restricted to the general editor. Both runs use FLUX.2-klein9B as the general editor and Qwen3.8-27B in all VLM roles. All distinct images generated in these runs form the pool of set, from which we keep up to four, giving priority to the delivered results and to methods not yet represented. This yields 2 to 4 candidates per set and 1,995 candidates in total. Annotation. Five professional Photoshop editors label each set together in shared interface and agree on one label, so each set has one consensus label. The interface shows the source image, the instruction and the candidates under neutral keys (C1 to C4), in an order fixed by hash and without any indication of their method. For each set, the editors select every usable candidate, i.e., every candidate that completes the instruction acceptably. usable candidate is selected even when another candidate is better, so an unselected candidate is unusable, not merely second best. The editors can also mark the set as all usable or all unusable. Of the 600 sets, 248 have one selected candidate, 155 have several, 116 are marked as all usable and 81 as all unusable. Winner-Set Hit@1. The winner set of set contains its selected candidates, or all candidates when the set is marked all usable. It is thus the set of usable candidates, and WinnerSet Hit@1 measures how often judges top choice is usable. We exclude the 81 sets without usable candidate. Of the remaining 519, we also exclude 4 in which one candidate has no verification record, so that every judge is compared on the same 515 sets. judge that scores candidates separately selects its top-scoring candidate. When several candidates share the top score, the tie is broken uniformly at random, and we count the expected outcome, i.e., the fraction of the tied candidates that are in the winner set. An invalid output, or missing score for any candidate of the set, counts as 0. Accuracy is computed per run over the fixed set of sets and averaged over three runs. The random baseline is the mean over sets of the winner-set size divided by the number of candidates. It is 59.32% on the 515 sets and 47.10% on the 396 sets with at least one unusable candidate.
